title: Influencing stakeholders
blurb: Choose the right influencing technique and the right level of engagement (inform, consult, involve, collaborate) for each stakeholder.
question: A hospital is introducing electronic staff rostering. A senior consultant, who has no reporting line to the project manager, is telling colleagues the system will not work. How can the project manager influence this stakeholder, and what level of engagement would suit them?

teach.h: Influence: moving people without the power to order them
teach.body: Influence is the ability to change what others think, decide or do. Project managers rarely have authority over sponsors, users, functional managers or suppliers, so they must influence rather than instruct. Effective influence rests on understanding: the stakeholder analysis tells you what each person cares about, what worries them and who they listen to. In plain English: you win people over by giving them good reasons, good relationships and a real say.

head: Technique
What it means
Example
rows: Make a reasoned case linked to their goals
Show how it cuts their overtime
Give them a real part in shaping it
Invite them to a design workshop
A trusted peer champions the change
Fit training around their busy period
Let facts and data make the case
Share results from a pilot site
teach.caption: Most real influence combines several techniques. Analysis tells you which will work for whom.

steps.label: Inform
steps.sub: One-way: tell them what is happening

steps.label: Consult
steps.sub: Ask for their views; the project decides

steps.label: Involve
steps.sub: Work with them; their input shapes options

teach.caption: Moving right gives stakeholders more say and builds more commitment, but takes more time and effort.

teach.h: Match the level to the stakeholder
teach.body: There is no single right level. Higher levels build ownership and reduce resistance, but they cost time and raise expectations that views will be acted on. Lower levels are efficient but can leave important people feeling ignored. Key players usually need involving or collaborating; interested but less powerful groups need informing and consulting. Never consult on something already decided: false consultation destroys trust faster than not asking.

teach.h: A typical match: grid quadrant to level
teach.caption: A starting point, not a fixed rule. A low-power group with vital expertise, such as end users, may still be involved.

teach.body: Dr Shah is resistant and influential. The project manager meets her one-to-one to understand her worry (building relationships): rotas set by software that ignores clinical cover. She is invited to the rules workshop (involving people). Results from the pilot ward show fewer gaps in cover (evidence). The ward sister she trusts speaks up for it (using allies). Her department goes live after its busiest month (reciprocity). Her level moves from inform to involve.

teach.h: Consult or involve? The commonest confusion

rows.label: Stakeholder role
values: Works on options with the team

rows.label: Who decides
values: The project, shaped by their input

teach.caption: Collaborate goes one step further: decisions are made jointly as partners.

rows.label: Evidence
values: Working increments shown each time box

teach.caption: Iterative work gives frequent, visible evidence; a demo of working software can persuade far better than a slide deck.

teach.text: Exam trap: 'consult' is NOT 'involve'. Consulting asks for views and the project decides; involving gives stakeholders a hand in shaping the options. And 'inform' is one-way only. Also beware options that treat higher levels as always better: the right level depends on the stakeholder.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Explain why influence is needed: the project manager lacks authority over most stakeholders.
Link it to analysis: influence depends on knowing interests, concerns and who they trust.
Name and apply techniques: persuasion, relationships, involvement, allies, reciprocity, evidence.
Choose a level: inform, consult, involve or collaborate, matched to power and interest.
Note the trade-off: more say builds commitment but costs time and raises expectations.
Influence = changing what people think or do without relying on authority.
Techniques: persuasion, building relationships, involving people, using allies, reciprocity, evidence.
Levels of engagement: inform → consult → involve → collaborate.
Higher levels build commitment but cost more time; match the level to the stakeholder.
Iterative projects use frequent demos as evidence and collaborate closely with users.

summary: You can now explain why project managers must influence rather than instruct, and choose from six influencing techniques. You can also pick a level of engagement from inform to collaborate that suits each stakeholder, weighing commitment against time and effort.

A.q: A project manager shares figures from a three-month pilot to convince a sceptical finance director that new software will save money. Which influencing technique is this?
A.why: Using facts and data, such as pilot results, to make the case is influencing through evidence.

whyNot.1: Reciprocity is offering something in return for something.
whyNot.2: Using allies means working through people the stakeholder trusts.
whyNot.3: Involvement means giving the stakeholder a part in shaping the work.

A.q: At which level of engagement are stakeholders asked for their views, but the project team makes the decision?
A.why: Consulting asks for feedback on proposals or drafts; the decision remains with the project.

whyNot.0: Informing is one-way: no views are sought.
whyNot.1: Collaborating makes decisions jointly with the stakeholder.
whyNot.3: Involving goes further than consulting: stakeholders work on shaping the options.

A.q: Why do project managers usually need to influence stakeholders rather than simply direct them?
options: Directing people is banned by governance
Influence avoids the need for a plan
They lack authority over most of them
A.why: Sponsors, functional managers, users and suppliers do not report to the project manager, so support has to be won through influence.

whyNot.0: Governance doesn't ban direction; the issue is that authority is limited.
whyNot.1: Formal reporting is often valued by stakeholders; this is not the reason.
whyNot.2: Influencing is planned in the engagement plan; it does not replace planning.

B.q: A project manager asks a well-respected team leader to talk positively about the new system with her colleagues. Which technique is being used?
B.why: Working through someone the stakeholders already trust and respect is using allies.

whyNot.0: Persuasion is the project manager making a reasoned case directly.
whyNot.2: Reciprocity is an exchange of favours or concessions.
whyNot.3: Involving people gives them a part in shaping the work; here a trusted peer speaks for it instead.

B.q: A warehouse manager agrees to release staff for testing after the project manager moves training away from his peak season. Which technique has the project manager used?
B.why: Giving something the stakeholder values (a better training date) in return for something the project needs (testers) is reciprocity.

whyNot.1: No trusted third party was used.
whyNot.2: No data or results were used to make the case.
whyNot.3: Persuasion is a reasoned argument; this was an exchange.

B.q: On an agile project, the product owner and team decide together which features go into each time box. Which level of engagement does this show?
B.why: Making decisions jointly, as partners with shared ownership, is collaboration.

whyNot.1: Informing is one-way and gives no say in decisions.
whyNot.2: Consulting seeks views but leaves the decision with the project.
whyNot.3: Keep satisfied is a power/interest grid quadrant, not a level of engagement.

C.q: A project manager runs a 'consultation' on a new office layout after the design has already been signed off. What is the most likely effect?
options: Stronger ownership of the final design
Faster acceptance of the new layout
Lost trust and more resistance to it
C.why: Asking for views that cannot change anything is false consultation: people realise their input was ignored, trust falls and resistance grows.

whyNot.0: Ownership comes from genuine involvement, not a token exercise.
whyNot.1: Token consultation tends to slow acceptance as people feel misled.
whyNot.2: Asking for views usually raises expectations that they will be acted on.

C.q: Which TWO statements about levels of engagement are correct? 1. Higher levels give stakeholders more say  2. Informing is a two-way process  3. Higher levels need more time and effort  4. Every stakeholder should be collaborated with
C.why: Moving from inform to collaborate gives stakeholders more say and builds commitment, but takes more time and effort.

whyNot.0: Informing is one-way, so statement 2 is wrong.
whyNot.2: Informing is one-way, and collaborating with everyone is impractical.
whyNot.3: Collaborating with everyone is impractical; the level must suit the stakeholder.

C.q: A union representative opposes a depot move because members fear longer journeys. Which approach is most likely to gain support?
options: Escalate to the sponsor to overrule him
Involve him in shaping shift patterns
Delay engagement until the move is done
C.why: His concern is real and he is influential, so involving him in shaping solutions addresses the concern and builds ownership.

whyNot.0: One-way updates do not address his members' concern.
whyNot.1: Overruling an influential stakeholder usually hardens resistance.
whyNot.3: Delaying engagement lets opposition grow and removes any chance to shape the outcome.

reteach.title: Getting your housemates to agree a cleaning rota
reteach.question: You want your shared house to adopt a cleaning rota, but you're not anyone's boss. How would you get everyone on board?

blocks.body: You can't order anyone, so you explain how a rota ends the arguments (persuasion). You show the photo of last week's kitchen (evidence). You ask the most popular housemate to back the idea (using allies). You offer to take the worst job for the first month (reciprocity). And you let everyone help design the rota rather than presenting a finished one (involving people). A rota people helped build is one they stick to.

blocks.h: How much say do they get?

steps.label: Inform
steps.sub: Pin the rota on the fridge

steps.label: Consult
steps.sub: Ask what they think of your draft

steps.label: Involve
steps.sub: Draft it together at a house meeting

blocks.text: Asking for comments on a rota you've already printed and laminated is false consultation. It annoys people more than not asking.

explain.body: Most stakeholders are outside the project manager's line of authority. Their support must be earned. Influence works best when it is based on the stakeholder analysis: their interests, concerns, attitude and who they trust.

test.q: What should the choice of influencing technique for a stakeholder mainly be based on?
test.why: Analysis of their interests, concerns, attitude and relationships shows which techniques are likely to work.

whyNot.0: Job title alone says little about what will persuade someone.
whyNot.2: Budget limits effort but does not tell you what will move a stakeholder.
whyNot.3: The sponsor's view may help, but the choice should rest on understanding the stakeholder.

explain.body: Persuasion makes a reasoned case linked to the stakeholder's own goals. Evidence lets facts carry the argument: pilot results, data, benchmarks, demonstrations. Both work best on stakeholders who respond to logic and proof.

rows.label: Example
values: Pilot cut errors by a third

test.q: Which technique relies mainly on facts and data to make the case?
test.why: Evidence uses facts, data and demonstrable results to make the case.

whyNot.0: Allies influence through trust in a person.
whyNot.2: Relationships influence through trust built over time.

explain.body: Building relationships earns trust over time. Involving people gives them a real part in shaping the work, so they own it. Using allies works through people the stakeholder respects. Reciprocity gives something the stakeholder values in return for their support.

test.q: A project manager offers a functional manager first use of the new equipment in return for releasing two engineers. Which technique is this?
test.why: Offering something valued in exchange for something the project needs is reciprocity.

whyNot.0: No trusted third party is involved.
whyNot.2: No data is being used to argue the case.
whyNot.3: The manager is not being given a role in shaping the work.

explain.body: Inform (one-way updates), consult (ask for views, project decides), involve (work together on options), collaborate (decide jointly as partners). The level should match the stakeholder's power, interest and value to the work.

test.q: Which level of engagement is one-way, with no views sought from stakeholders?
test.why: Informing simply tells stakeholders what is happening; no feedback is sought.

whyNot.1: Involving works with stakeholders on options.
